transcript.content: Hi, welcome in, I'm Dr. [name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I’m here because something’s been going on with the environmental modeling contract I’m working on. I do mathematical modeling, mostly, and I’ve led work like this before—though people act like I haven’t, which is sort of the point.

I’m pretty sure some of the people on that contract are tracking my revisions, watching what I change, and then planting errors in the datasets so it looks like I’m the one who can’t keep the work straight. My wife says it’s probably just version-control mistakes, and the junior analysts say the same thing, but they don’t see the pattern. I mean, version control doesn’t just repeatedly make me look incompetent right before reviews. That’s why I came in.
How long have you been noticing this pattern of people tracking your work and planting errors—days, weeks, or longer?

Longer than days or weeks, really. I’d say it’s been about two months that I’ve been sure they’re tracking my revisions and slipping errors into the data. It started out looking like ordinary mistakes, but then the timing—well, the timing kept lining up with reviews and it was just too consistent.
During these past two months, have you experienced anything like hearing voices, seeing things, or other unusual sensory experiences that others don't seem to notice?

I don’t know that I’d call it hearing voices or seeing things, exactly. I mean, the computer makes noises, the building has those little hums—servers, fluorescent lights, all that—and after you’ve worked late enough everything sort of blends together. Back when I was doing finite element stuff, you could almost tell from the fan pitch when a run was going bad, which sounds strange but it’s true.

But, uh… no, I haven’t really noticed things like seeing something other people don’t see. Not in that sense. The issue is more the pattern in the work files.
Over these past two months, have you also noticed changes in your mood—like feeling unusually depressed, hopeless, or on the other end, unusually elevated, energetic, or needing much less sleep?

I’m not sure I’d put it in those terms. I mean, anybody would get discouraged when people keep acting like your work is sloppy, especially when you’ve spent years learning how to catch numerical problems before they propagate. There was this one project years ago where a tiny rounding issue threw off a whole model, and everyone blamed the inputs first—

But mood, like depressed or elevated… I don’t know. I’ve been stressed, I guess. Annoyed. Tired sometimes because I’m thinking about the files and what they’re doing with them. But I haven’t really been tracking it as a mood thing.
Aside from the concerns about your work files, have you noticed any change in how you're managing other parts of your daily life—like relationships, self-care, or other responsibilities?

Yeah… I mean, I’ve tried to keep the rest of things normal, but it’s gotten messy. At work I’m behind on the modeling deliverables—far enough behind that the firm started reassigning parts of the contract to other people. And I’m supposed to be supervising the junior analysts, helping them catch mistakes, but lately I’m not really useful to them.

At home, I mostly keep to myself. My wife has been on me about basic routines—meals, getting moving, just keeping things in order. It’s not that I’m trying to let things slide, it’s just… once you’re watching the files and trying to reconstruct what happened, hours disappear.

Before these past two months when things became clear to you, did you notice any earlier signs—even subtle ones, like feeling unusually suspicious of colleagues, or acting or thinking differently than your usual self—going back further, say four to six months ago?

Four to six months… I don’t know. I mean, I’ve always been careful with revisions. In modeling work you have to be, because one bad change can sit there unnoticed and then suddenly the whole thing is off—people think it’s just a formatting issue, but it’s not.

But the part where I was really sure people on the project were tracking my revisions and putting errors into the files… that’s more like the last two months. Before that, maybe I was irritated or watching things more closely, but it wasn’t clear to me the way it is now.

Over these past two months, has this belief that your colleagues are tracking your revisions and planting errors been present continuously the whole time, or have there been any stretches—even a few days—where that belief went away or felt less certain?

It hasn’t really gone away, no. I mean, some hours I’m not actively thinking about it—if I’m eating dinner or my wife is talking about something with the house—but then I look back at the files and it’s right there again.

People keep saying “version control,” like that explains everything, but I’ve worked with datasets long enough to know when something is being changed after the fact. The junior analysts act like it’s just confusion, and my wife wants me to step away from it, but… I’m pretty sure they’ve been tracking my revisions and putting errors in to make it look like I can’t lead the contract. So, no, I wouldn’t say there’s been a stretch where I stopped believing it.

Yeah, it’s been about two months that I’ve been sure about it. I mean, before that I was checking things more carefully, but the part where it clicked—where it was obvious to me they were tracking my revisions and planting errors—that’s been these last couple months.

It’s hard to put an exact day on it, because with project files everything kind of blurs together. You open one spreadsheet, then another, then you’re comparing timestamps, and suddenly it’s midnight. But roughly… yeah, about two months.
Over these past two months, have you been using any alcohol, recreational drugs, or new medications/supplements—including changes in caffeine or stimulant use?

I don’t think there’s anything like that that explains it. I mean, I have coffee like most people do—though honestly coffee in offices has gotten ridiculous, those little pods and people leaving them everywhere, and then everyone acts surprised when the kitchenette smells burnt.

But, no, I’m not… I’m not taking some new thing to make me think this. I’d have to look at the exact dates if you mean every supplement bottle in the cabinet. My wife buys vitamins sometimes and they end up in a drawer. I’m not sure what counts there. But recreational drugs, no. Alcohol isn’t really a major thing for me. Nothing that jumps out as a change.

Have your wife or coworkers mentioned noticing anything unusual in how you're speaking or organizing your thoughts, or have you felt less motivated, more flat, or withdrawn in ways that go beyond just this situation with the files?

My wife has said I’ve been… harder to talk to, I guess. Not in those words exactly. More like I’m sitting there but not really there.

And yeah, I suppose I have pulled back. I can sit for hours at my desk, or out in the garage, and the telescope is right there still covered. I used to go to those astronomy nights, and hiking too, and I liked mentoring the younger analysts—well, some of them, when they actually wanted to learn and not just click around in dashboards like the software is doing the thinking for them.

But lately I just don’t feel much pull to start any of it. Even talking to people feels like too much effort sometimes. It’s not only the files, though the files make everything worse. It’s like I know what I used to do, but I don’t feel the push to do it.

Thinking back, did this sense of low energy, pulling away from people, and losing interest in things like the telescope and mentoring start around the same time you became sure about the revision-tracking, or did you notice that happening earlier, before you were sure about the pattern in the files?

It was earlier than the part where I was sure about the files. The whole… decline, I guess you’d call it, started after they put me in charge of that larger environmental modeling contract.

That was about two years and two months ago. Funny how I can remember that more clearly than what I had for dinner yesterday, because the contract dates were all in those binders and kickoff meetings, and everyone suddenly had opinions about runoff coefficients like they’d been studying them their whole lives.

But yes, before I was sure about the revision-tracking, I was already pulling back. That bigger contract was when things started going downhill.

I’m not sure I can slice it that cleanly, honestly. It all sort of runs together when I look back on it. I can tell something was off before I was really focused on the file issue, but putting exact order on feelings is harder than putting dates on contracts or emails.

I mean, with paperwork you can line it up—version one, version two, timestamps, who touched what. With yourself it’s not like that. One day you just realize you haven’t called someone back, or you walked past something you used to enjoy and didn’t even think to use it. So… I don’t know if I can give you a sharper answer than that.

inference.note: Added F20 given emerging negative symptoms (avolition, social withdrawal, flattened affect, functional decline) alongside a fixed persecutory delusion for ~2 months, which raises concern for schizophrenia rather than isolated delusional disorder. F25 and F32.3 remain considerations given possible mood component (anhedonia, withdrawal) that could be primary rather than secondary to the delusional stress; further mood-timeline clarification needed to rule these in/out.

doctor.question: Thinking back, did this sense of low energy, pulling away from people, and losing interest in things like the telescope and mentoring start around the same time you became sure about the revision-tracking, or did you notice that happening earlier, before you were sure about the pattern in the files?

patient.answer:
It was earlier than the part where I was sure about the files. The whole… decline, I guess you’d call it, started after they put me in charge of that larger environmental modeling contract.

That was about two years and two months ago. Funny how I can remember that more clearly than what I had for dinner yesterday, because the contract dates were all in those binders and kickoff meetings, and everyone suddenly had opinions about runoff coefficients like they’d been studying them their whole lives.

But yes, before I was sure about the revision-tracking, I was already pulling back. That bigger contract was when things started going downhill.

inference.note: Patient denies depressed/elevated mood despite direct questioning, making a mood disorder with psychotic features less likely, so F32.3 is dropped. The clear 2+ year prodrome of functional decline, avolition, and social withdrawal preceding the fixed persecutory delusion, combined with negative symptoms and significant occupational/social impairment, favors F20 over an isolated delusional disorder, though F22 and F25 remain possible pending clarification of mood symptom timing/severity.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I can slice it that cleanly, honestly. It all sort of runs together when I look back on it. I can tell something was off before I was really focused on the file issue, but putting exact order on feelings is harder than putting dates on contracts or emails.

I mean, with paperwork you can line it up—version one, version two, timestamps, who touched what. With yourself it’s not like that. One day you just realize you haven’t called someone back, or you walked past something you used to enjoy and didn’t even think to use it. So… I don’t know if I can give you a sharper answer than that.

inference.note: The 2+ year history of functional decline, social withdrawal, anhedonia, and blunted affect preceding the onset of the persecutory delusions argues against delusional disorder (F22), which requires isolated delusions without prominent negative symptoms or functional deterioration. The patient explicitly denies any distinct mood episode (depressive or manic) concurrent with the psychotic symptoms, making schizoaffective disorder (F25) unlikely. The combination of prodromal negative symptoms with over 6 months of overall illness duration, active persecutory delusions for 2 months, and functional decline fits schizophrenia (F20) best.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient displays a fixed, non-bizarre-but-firmly-held persecutory delusion (coworkers tracking and sabotaging his data) persisting continuously for 2 months, meeting active-phase criteria. Crucially, this is embedded in a much longer prodromal course (~2 years) marked by social withdrawal, anhedonia (abandoning astronomy/hiking/mentoring), flat/blunted interpersonal engagement ('sitting there but not really there'), and progressive occupational decline (falling behind, being reassigned work, reduced ability to supervise junior staff). No manic or depressive episode was identified to account for the psychosis (ruling out schizoaffective disorder), and the presence of prominent negative symptoms and functional deterioration over more than 6 months distinguishes this from an isolated delusional disorder (F22), which typically lacks such marked negative symptoms and functional decline. Substance use and organic/medication causes were denied and no perceptual disturbances (hallucinations) were confirmed, though negative symptoms and one delusion are sufficient given functional impairment and duration >6 months. This presentation is best explained by schizophrenia (F20).
